validator: draft 1 passed with no hard or soft problems (whatAmILookingAt 11408 characters). The faults below are the critic's.
keep: The idea is named up front in one plain sentence: flow runs only along a path open all the way through a running pump, so read the valves and pumps, then trace.
DOE's flowpath-for-a-lineup reading is the shape: the job, the parts, the drawn state, then the lineup traced, then isolation.

Fourteen screens alternate SHOW and DO, opening on a typed recall from Heat and fluids lesson 8 (a pump against a shut valve: full head, no flow) that sets up the rule, and ending on two mixed puzzles on the fuel sheet (13, 14).

Each misconception in the brief that RESEARCH can carry has a DO screen with its own hint: the drawn state read as running (3), water assumed to run back through a stopped pump (5), a three-way valve read as a shut-off (7), one side of an isolation missed and a non-return valve trusted as one (9, 14), the drawing trusted over the plant (11), and a cross-connection's second path missed (13, 14).
Only the recall's head and the strainer's valve count are figures, so they are the only typed answers, each with its slips. The rest are taps or named choices.
Safety comes first in practice: lock off the pump, shut and lock a valve on every pipe, never a non-return valve, then drain and prove at zero.
The trade analogy (a starter with a separate control supply) is new to the course, reproduces the main result and echoes the course's opening puzzle.
fix: False absolute: 'water moves only along a path that is open all the way through a running pump' is not true of the real world. A tank above the line, or trapped pressure, also drives flow, and the fuel sheet's tanks would. Say it of a pumped system, and add that a higher tank or trapped pressure can push flow too, which is one more reason to isolate on every side.

Causal step skipped: explain and screen 5 say water could pass back through P2's casing, but not why it would. Add that P1's discharge sits at a higher pressure than the suction, so any open way between them carries water back.
Causal step skipped: screen 11's why says the expanding water has nowhere to go, but the header tank was only said to keep the loop full. Say it also gives the water room to expand.
Full head against a shut valve is a centrifugal pump's behaviour. Say P1 and P2 are centrifugal pumps, like the earlier one.

A source's vocabulary: 'Check every isolation point on the plant against the line diagram' copies HSG253's words. Put it in plain words: walk the plant and check that each valve you will use is on the drawing, where the drawing says.
Overclaim: 'A valve on the plant that the drawing does not show changes the paths without warning' is true only when it is shut. Say it can change them.
Isolate mode's reason 'cannot be locked' is given for a stopped pump too, which is wrong: its starter can be. Give each its own reason.
Unreadable labels: about seventeen tags on one loop at 340 px. Lay the loop out tall at phone width, and let the tags sit outside the lines.
Explain's second paragraph runs long. Split the lineup trace from the parts, so it reads as four short paragraphs.
Rule of thumb 'each one needs a shut valve' should say each pipe that leads anywhere, since a capped stub needs none.
